Researchers have successfully transferred the knowledge of a large, complex group of machine learning models into a single, compact model [P3_p1_c03]. 

Training many different models together creates great results, but running them all at once is too expensive for everyday users [P3_p1_c02]. To solve this problem, scientists use a new technique called distillation [P3_p1_c03]. Distillation transfers the hidden knowledge from a cumbersome group of models into one small model that is much easier to deploy [P3_p1_c03]. 

For example, when recognizing handwritten digits, a large model might assign tiny probabilities showing how a specific two might slightly resemble a three or a seven [P3_p2_c04]. This rich similarity information is normally lost, but distillation captures it by raising the temperature of the model to produce soft targets [P3_p2_c04]. 

This method achieves surprising results on image tasks and significantly improves the acoustic model of a heavily used commercial system [P3_p1_c02]. More than 80% of the accuracy improvement gained by using an ensemble of 10 models is successfully transferred to the single distilled model [P3_p5_c02]. 

This breakthrough matters because it bridges the gap between heavy training needs and the strict speed requirements of real-world users [P3_p1_c03].
